file.content:
# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

file.content:
# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

content.content:
1→# rlibc-x
     2→
     3→A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.
     4→
     5→## Goals
     6→
     7→- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
     8→- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
     9→- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`
    10→
    11→## Results
    12→
    13→The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:
    14→
    15→```
    16→$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
    17→-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1
    18→
    19→$ file target/release/ex-x1
    20→ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
    21→```
    22→
    23→This is achieved through:
    24→- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
    25→- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
    26→- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
    27→- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
    28→- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols
    29→
    30→For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.
    31→
    32→See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.
    33→
    34→## Workspace Structure
    35→
    36→| Directory | Description |
    37→|-----------|-------------|
    38→| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
    39→| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
    40→| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
    41→| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
    42→| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |
    43→
    44→## Two Approaches
    45→
    46→**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.
    47→
    48→**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.
    49→
    50→## Quick Start
    51→
    52→```bash
    53→# Build and run
    54→cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
    55→cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2
    56→
    57→# Test
    58→cargo xtask test               # run all tests
    59→cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode
    60→
    61→# Build release
    62→cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
    63→```
    64→
    65→For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)
    66→
    67→## Verifying No libc Usage
    68→
    69→The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:
    70→
    71→```bash
    72→cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
    73→cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
    74→```
    75→
    76→All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.
    77→
    78→## Status
    79→
    80→This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:
    81→
    82→- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
    83→- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust
    84→
    85→## Origin
    86→
    87→Started with this prompt for Claude Code:
    88→
    89→> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
    90→> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
    91→> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
    92→> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."
    93→
    94→Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.
    95→
    96→## License
    97→

    99→
   100→- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
   101→- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
   102→

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

file.content:
# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

content.content:
1→# rlibc-x
     2→
     3→A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.
     4→
     5→## Goals
     6→
     7→- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
     8→- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
     9→- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`
    10→
    11→## Results
    12→
    13→The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:
    14→
    15→```
    16→$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
    17→-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1
    18→
    19→$ file target/release/ex-x1
    20→ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
    21→```
    22→
    23→This is achieved through:
    24→- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
    25→- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
    26→- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
    27→- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
    28→- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols
    29→
    30→For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.
    31→
    32→See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.
    33→
    34→## Workspace Structure

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

file.content:
# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

1→# rlibc-x
     2→
     3→A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.
     4→
     5→## Goals
     6→
     7→- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
     8→- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
     9→- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`
    10→
    11→## Results
    12→
    13→The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:
    14→
    15→```
    16→$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
    17→-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1
    18→
    19→$ file target/release/ex-x1
    20→ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
    21→```
    22→
    23→This is achieved through:
    24→- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
    25→- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
    26→- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
    27→- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
    28→- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols
    29→
    30→For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.
    31→
    32→See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.
    33→
    34→## Workspace Structure
    35→
    36→| Directory | Description |
    37→|-----------|-------------|
    38→| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
    39→| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
    40→| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
    41→| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
    42→| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |
    43→
    44→## Two Approaches
    45→
    46→**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.
    47→
    48→**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.
    49→
    50→## Quick Start
    51→
    52→```bash
    53→# Build and run
    54→cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
    55→cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2
    56→
    57→# Test
    58→cargo xtask test               # run all tests
    59→cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode
    60→
    61→# Build release
    62→cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
    63→```
    64→
    65→For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)
    66→
    67→## Verifying No libc Usage
    68→
    69→The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:
    70→
    71→```bash
    72→cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
    73→cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
    74→```
    75→
    76→All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.
    77→
    78→## Status
    79→
    80→This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:
    81→
    82→- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
    83→- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust
    84→
    85→## Origin
    86→
    87→Started with this prompt for Claude Code:
    88→
    89→> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
    90→> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
    91→> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
    92→> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."
    93→
    94→Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

content.content:
1→# rlibc-x
     2→
     3→A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.
     4→
     5→## Goals
     6→
     7→- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
     8→- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
     9→- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`
    10→
    11→## Results
    12→
    13→The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:
    14→
    15→```
    16→$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
    17→-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1
    18→
    19→$ file target/release/ex-x1
    20→ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
    21→```
    22→
    23→This is achieved through:
    24→- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
    25→- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
    26→- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
    27→- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
    28→- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols
    29→
    30→For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.
    31→
    32→See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.
    33→
    34→## Workspace Structure
    35→
    36→| Directory | Description |
    37→|-----------|-------------|
    38→| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
    39→| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
    40→| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
    41→| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
    42→| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |
    43→
    44→## Two Approaches
    45→
    46→**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.
    47→
    48→**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.
    49→
    50→## Quick Start
    51→
    52→```bash
    53→# Build and run
    54→cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
    55→cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2
    56→
    57→# Test
    58→cargo xtask test               # run all tests
    59→cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode
    60→
    61→# Build release
    62→cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
    63→```
    64→
    65→For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)
    66→
    67→## Verifying No libc Usage
    68→
    69→The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:
    70→
    71→```bash
    72→cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
    73→cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
    74→```
    75→
    76→All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.
    77→
    78→## Status
    79→
    80→This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:
    81→
    82→- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
    83→- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust
    84→
    85→## Origin
    86→
    87→Started with this prompt for Claude Code:
    88→
    89→> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
    90→> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
    91→> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.
