# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# Example and Comparison Apps

Binary size comparison across different runtimes.

## Size Comparison

| App | Runtime | Linking | Size | Description |
|-----|---------|---------|-----:|-------------|
| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (no_std + no_main) |
| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 41.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (std with custom libc) |
| ex-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 283.7 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| ex-musl | musl | static | 372.6 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.5 KB | Hello world |
| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 45.8 KB | Hello world |
| hw-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 286.7 KB | Hello world |
| hw-musl | musl | static | 376.6 KB | Hello world |

## App Naming Convention

- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
- **-musl** = uses musl libc

## Building and Running

```bash
# Using xtask (recommended)
cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # build and run

# Direct cargo commands

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

1→//! Raw syscall wrappers for Linux x86_64
     2→
     3→use core::arch::asm;
     4→
     5→/// Invoke a syscall with 0 arguments.
     6→///
     7→/// # Safety
     8→/// Caller must ensure `n` is a valid syscall number and that invoking
     9→/// this syscall is safe in the current context.
    10→#[inline(always)]
    11→pub unsafe fn syscall0(n: u64) -> u64 {
    12→    let ret: u64;
    13→    unsafe {
    14→        asm!(

# Example and Comparison Apps

Binary size comparison across different runtimes.

## Size Comparison

| App | Runtime | Linking | Size | Description |
|-----|---------|---------|-----:|-------------|
| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (no_std + no_main) |
| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 41.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (std with custom libc) |
| ex-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 283.7 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| ex-musl | musl | static | 372.6 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.5 KB | Hello world |
| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 45.8 KB | Hello world |
| hw-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 286.7 KB | Hello world |
| hw-musl | musl | static | 376.6 KB | Hello world |

## App Naming Convention

- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
- **-musl** = uses musl libc

## Building and Running

```bash
# Using xtask (recommended)
cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # build and run

# Direct cargo commands
cargo build -p ex-x1 --release
cargo run -p hw-x1 --release

# glibc/musl targets (use aliases)
cargo b-glibc -p ex-glibc --release
cargo b-musl -p ex-musl --release
```

## Testing

Each app includes a test that verifies it doesn't use libc (for x1/x2 variants):

```bash
cargo xtask test ex-x1 hw-x1   # test specific apps
cargo xtask test               # test all
```

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

# Example and Comparison Apps

Binary size comparison across different runtimes.

## Size Comparison

| App | Runtime | Linking | Size | Description |
|-----|---------|---------|-----:|-------------|
| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (no_std + no_main) |
| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 41.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (std with custom libc) |
| ex-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 283.7 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| ex-musl | musl | static | 372.6 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.5 KB | Hello world |
| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 45.8 KB | Hello world |
| hw-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 286.7 KB | Hello world |
| hw-musl | musl | static | 376.6 KB | Hello world |

## App Naming Convention

- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
- **-musl** = uses musl libc

## Building and Running

```bash
# Using xtask (recommended)
cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # build and run

# Direct cargo commands
cargo build -p ex-x1 --release
cargo run -p hw-x1 --release

# glibc/musl targets (use aliases)
cargo b-glibc -p ex-glibc --release
cargo b-musl -p ex-musl --release
```

## Testing

Each app includes a test that verifies it doesn't use libc (for x1/x2 variants):

```bash
cargo xtask test ex-x1 hw-x1   # test specific apps
cargo xtask test               # test all
```

content.content:
1→# rlibc-x
     2→
     3→A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.
     4→
     5→## Goals
     6→
     7→- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
     8→- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
     9→- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`
    10→
    11→## Results
    12→
    13→The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:
    14→
    15→```
    16→$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
    17→-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1
    18→
    19→$ file target/release/ex-x1
    20→ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
    21→```
    22→
    23→This is achieved through:
    24→- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
    25→- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
    26→- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
    27→- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
    28→- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols
    29→
    30→For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.
    31→
    32→See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.
    33→
    34→## Workspace Structure
    35→
    36→| Directory | Description |
    37→|-----------|-------------|
    38→| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
    39→| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
    40→| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
    41→| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
    42→| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |
    43→
    44→## Two Approaches
    45→
    46→**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.
    47→
    48→**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.
    49→
    50→## Quick Start
    51→
    52→```bash
    53→# Build and run
    54→cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
    55→cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2
    56→
    57→# Test
    58→cargo xtask test               # run all tests
    59→cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode
    60→
    61→# Build release
    62→cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
    63→```
    64→
    65→For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)
    66→
    67→## Verifying No libc Usage
    68→
    69→The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

# Example and Comparison Apps

Binary size comparison across different runtimes.

## Size Comparison

| App | Runtime | Linking | Size | Description |
|-----|---------|---------|-----:|-------------|
| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (no_std + no_main) |
| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 41.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (std with custom libc) |
| ex-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 283.7 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| ex-musl | musl | static | 372.6 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.5 KB | Hello world |
| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 45.8 KB | Hello world |
| hw-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 286.7 KB | Hello world |
| hw-musl | musl | static | 376.6 KB | Hello world |

## App Naming Convention

- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
- **-musl** = uses musl libc

## Building and Running

```bash
# Using xtask (recommended)
cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # build and run

# Direct cargo commands
cargo build -p ex-x1 --release
cargo run -p hw-x1 --release

# glibc/musl targets (use aliases)
cargo b-glibc -p ex-glibc --release
cargo b-musl -p ex-musl --release
```

## Testing

Each app includes a test that verifies it doesn't use libc (for x1/x2 variants):

```bash
cargo xtask test ex-x1 hw-x1   # test specific apps
cargo xtask test               # test all
```

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

# Example and Comparison Apps

Binary size comparison across different runtimes.

## Size Comparison

| App | Runtime | Linking | Size | Description |
|-----|---------|---------|-----:|-------------|
| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (no_std + no_main) |
| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 41.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (std with custom libc) |
| ex-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 283.7 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| ex-musl | musl | static | 372.6 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.5 KB | Hello world |
| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 45.8 KB | Hello world |
| hw-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 286.7 KB | Hello world |
| hw-musl | musl | static | 376.6 KB | Hello world |

## App Naming Convention

- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
- **-musl** = uses musl libc

## Building and Running

```bash
# Using xtask (recommended)
cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # build and run

# Direct cargo commands
cargo build -p ex-x1 --release
cargo run -p hw-x1 --release

# glibc/musl targets (use aliases)
cargo b-glibc -p ex-glibc --release
cargo b-musl -p ex-musl --release
```

## Testing

Each app includes a test that verifies it doesn't use libc (for x1/x2 variants):

```bash
cargo xtask test ex-x1 hw-x1   # test specific apps
cargo xtask test               # test all
```

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

    18→## App Naming Convention
    19→
    20→- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
    21→- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
    22→- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
    23→- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
    24→- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
    25→- **-musl** = uses musl libc
    26→
    27→## Building and Running
    28→
    29→```bash
    30→# Using xtask (recommended)
    31→cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
    32→cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build
    33→cargo xtask run hw-x1          # build and run
    34→
    35→# Direct cargo commands
    36→cargo build -p ex-x1 --release
    37→cargo run -p hw-x1 --release
    38→
    39→# glibc/musl targets (use aliases)
    40→cargo b-glibc -p ex-glibc --release
    41→cargo b-musl -p ex-musl --release
    42→```

Binary size comparison across different runtimes.

## Size Comparison

| App | Runtime | Linking | Size | Description |
|-----|---------|---------|-----:|-------------|
| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (no_std + no_main) |
| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 41.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (std with custom libc) |
| ex-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 283.7 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| ex-musl | musl | static | 372.6 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.5 KB | Hello world |
| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 45.8 KB | Hello world |
| hw-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 286.7 KB | Hello world |
| hw-musl | musl | static | 376.6 KB | Hello world |

## App Naming Convention

- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
- **-musl** = uses musl libc

cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build

cargo run -p hw-x1 --release

```

Each app includes a test that verifies it doesn't use libc (for x1/x2 variants):

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall
be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# Example and Comparison Apps

Binary size comparison across different runtimes.

## Size Comparison

| App | Runtime | Linking | Size | Description |
|-----|---------|---------|-----:|-------------|
| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (no_std + no_main) |
| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 41.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (std with custom libc) |
| ex-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 283.7 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| ex-musl | musl | static | 372.6 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.5 KB | Hello world |
| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 45.8 KB | Hello world |
| hw-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 286.7 KB | Hello world |
| hw-musl | musl | static | 376.6 KB | Hello world |

## App Naming Convention

- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
- **-musl** = uses musl libc

## Building and Running

```bash
# Using xtask (recommended)
cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # build and run

# Direct cargo commands
cargo build -p ex-x1 --release
cargo run -p hw-x1 --release

# glibc/musl targets (use aliases)
cargo b-glibc -p ex-glibc --release
cargo b-musl -p ex-musl --release
```

## Testing

Each app includes a test that verifies it doesn't use libc (for x1/x2 variants):

```bash
cargo xtask test ex-x1 hw-x1   # test specific apps
cargo xtask test               # test all
```

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or http://apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

1→//! Raw syscall wrappers for Linux x86_64
     2→
     3→use core::arch::asm;
     4→
     5→/// Invoke a syscall with 0 arguments.
     6→///
     7→/// # Safety
     8→/// Caller must ensure `n` is a valid syscall number and that invoking
     9→/// this syscall is safe in the current context.
    10→#[inline(always)]
    11→pub unsafe fn syscall0(n: u64) -> u64 {
    12→    let ret: u64;
    13→    unsafe {
    14→        asm!(
    15→            "syscall",
    16→            in("rax") n,
    17→            lateout("rax") ret,
    18→            lateout("rcx") _,
    19→            lateout("r11") _,
    20→            options(nostack)

# Example and Comparison Apps

Binary size comparison across different runtimes.

## Size Comparison

| App | Runtime | Linking | Size | Description |
|-----|---------|---------|-----:|-------------|
| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (no_std + no_main) |
| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 41.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (std with custom libc) |
| ex-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 283.7 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| ex-musl | musl | static | 372.6 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.5 KB | Hello world |
| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 45.8 KB | Hello world |
| hw-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 286.7 KB | Hello world |
| hw-musl | musl | static | 376.6 KB | Hello world |

## App Naming Convention

- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
- **-musl** = uses musl libc

## Building and Running

```bash
# Using xtask (recommended)
cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # build and run

# Direct cargo commands
cargo build -p ex-x1 --release
cargo run -p hw-x1 --release

# glibc/musl targets (use aliases)
cargo b-glibc -p ex-glibc --release
cargo b-musl -p ex-musl --release
```

## Testing

Each app includes a test that verifies it doesn't use libc (for x1/x2 variants):

```bash
cargo xtask test ex-x1 hw-x1   # test specific apps
cargo xtask test               # test all
```

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

# Example and Comparison Apps

Binary size comparison across different runtimes.

## Size Comparison

| App | Runtime | Linking | Size | Description |
|-----|---------|---------|-----:|-------------|
| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (no_std + no_main) |
| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 41.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (std with custom libc) |
| ex-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 283.7 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| ex-musl | musl | static | 372.6 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.5 KB | Hello world |
| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 45.8 KB | Hello world |
| hw-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 286.7 KB | Hello world |
| hw-musl | musl | static | 376.6 KB | Hello world |

## App Naming Convention

- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
- **-musl** = uses musl libc

## Building and Running

```bash
# Using xtask (recommended)
cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # build and run

# Direct cargo commands
cargo build -p ex-x1 --release
cargo run -p hw-x1 --release

# glibc/musl targets (use aliases)
cargo b-glibc -p ex-glibc --release
cargo b-musl -p ex-musl --release
```

## Testing

Each app includes a test that verifies it doesn't use libc (for x1/x2 variants):

```bash
cargo xtask test ex-x1 hw-x1   # test specific apps
cargo xtask test               # test all
```

# rlibc-x

A minimal, educational Rust libc implementation for Linux x86_64.

## Goals

- **Educational** - Understand how Rust programs start, allocate memory, and interact with the kernel
- **Minimal binaries** - Explore whether simpler implementations can produce smaller binaries
- **Eventually transparent** - Long-term goal is to not require `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`

## Results

The rlibc-x1 + no_std approach produces a **1,480 byte** statically-linked executable:

```
$ cargo build -p ex-x1 --release && ls -la target/release/ex-x1
-rwxr-xr-x 2 wink users 1480 Jan 15 11:52 target/release/ex-x1

$ file target/release/ex-x1
ex-x1: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
```

This is achieved through:
- **`#![no_std]`** - No Rust standard library overhead
- **Direct syscalls** - `_start` → `_start_rust()` → `main()` → `exit()`
- **Bump allocator** - Simple `malloc`/`realloc` via `brk()`, `free()` is a no-op
- **`panic="abort"`** - No unwinding machinery
- **Aggressive optimization** - `opt-level='z'`, LTO, single codegen unit, stripped symbols

For comparison, rlibc-x2 (which supports `std`) produces ~41KB binaries.

See [apps/](apps/README.md#size-comparison) for the full size comparison across rlibc-x1, rlibc-x2, glibc, and musl.

## Workspace Structure

| Directory | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [rlibc-x1/](rlibc-x1/) | `#![no_std]` runtime (~1.4 KB binaries) |
| [rlibc-x2/](rlibc-x2/) | `std`-compatible libc replacement (~41 KB binaries) |
| [apps/](apps/) | Example and comparison apps |
| [tools/](tools/) | Development tools (`is-libc-used`) |
| [xtask/](xtask/) | Project automation |

## Two Approaches

**rlibc-x1** (no_std): App uses `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]`. Minimal, but requires explicit annotations.

**rlibc-x2** (std): App uses normal `fn main()` with Rust std. Replaces glibc while keeping std functionality.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Build and run
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # hello world with rlibc-x1
cargo xtask run hw-x2          # hello world with rlibc-x2

# Test
cargo xtask test               # run all tests
cargo xtask test -q            # quiet mode

# Build release
cargo xtask build -r           # release builds
```

For more information see [xtask/README.md](xtask/README.md)

## Verifying No libc Usage

The `is-libc-used` tool checks if a binary uses libc:

```bash
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- ./target/release/ex-x1
cargo run -p is-libc-used -- -v ./target/release/ex-x1  # verbose
```

All apps include libc usage tests that run with `cargo xtask test`.

## Status

This is an experimental/educational project. For production use, consider:

- [relibc](https://gitlab.redox-os.org/redox-os/relibc) - Redox OS's portable POSIX C library in Rust
- [c-ward](https://github.com/aspect-build/c-ward) - A libc implementation in Rust

## Origin

Started with this prompt for Claude Code:

> "I want to create a rust app that simply returns a number, something like `fn main -> i32 { 2 }`.
> I want to supply all code including the "standard libraries". I don't want the complication of
> code unwinding so panic="abort". So the minimum set of functions in lib.rs is _start, panic,
> exit, free, malloc, realloc, exit and probably a few others."

Initial versions created with Claude Code and ChatGPT. See [this ChatGPT conversation](https://chatgpt.com/share/695b4ae1-d84c-800c-8d09-34cff3de3b33) for the custom target approach.

## License

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

### Contribution

# Example and Comparison Apps

Binary size comparison across different runtimes.

## Size Comparison

| App | Runtime | Linking | Size | Description |
|-----|---------|---------|-----:|-------------|
| ex-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (no_std + no_main) |
| ex-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 41.4 KB | Minimal exit-only (std with custom libc) |
| ex-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 283.7 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| ex-musl | musl | static | 372.6 KB | Minimal exit-only |
| hw-x1 | rlibc-x1 | static | 1.5 KB | Hello world |
| hw-x2 | rlibc-x2 | static | 45.8 KB | Hello world |
| hw-glibc | glibc | dynamic | 286.7 KB | Hello world |
| hw-musl | musl | static | 376.6 KB | Hello world |

## App Naming Convention

- **ex-** = exit-only (just returns an exit code)
- **hw-** = hello world (prints to stdout)
- **-x1** = uses rlibc-x1 (no_std)
- **-x2** = uses rlibc-x2 (std)
- **-glibc** = uses system glibc
- **-musl** = uses musl libc

## Building and Running

```bash
# Using xtask (recommended)
cargo xtask build ex-x1        # debug build
cargo xtask build ex-x1 -r     # release build
cargo xtask run hw-x1          # build and run

# Direct cargo commands
cargo build -p ex-x1 --release
cargo run -p hw-x1 --release

# glibc/musl targets (use aliases)
cargo b-glibc -p ex-glibc --release
cargo b-musl -p ex-musl --release
```

## Testing

Each app includes a test that verifies it doesn't use libc (for x1/x2 variants):

```bash
cargo xtask test ex-x1 hw-x1   # test specific apps
cargo xtask test               # test all
```

## Comprehensive Codebase Exploration Report

### 1. Project Purpose

**rlibc-x** is an experimental, educational Rust implementation of libc for Linux x86_64. The project explores whether custom minimal libc implementations can produce significantly smaller binaries while maintaining Rust standard library compatibility. It achieves its smallest binaries at **1,480 bytes** for statically-linked executables (vs. 286KB+ for glibc/musl).

**Three core goals:**
- **Educational**: Understand Rust program initialization, memory allocation, and kernel interaction
- **Minimize binaries**: Explore smaller implementations through simplified approaches
- **Transparent replacement**: Eventually not require explicit `#![no_std]` and `#![no_main]` annotations

---

### 2. Overall Architecture and Structure

The project uses a **dual-implementation strategy** with a **workspace layout**:

```
rlibc-x/ (Workspace root)
├── rlibc-x1/           # Minimal no_std implementation (~1.4 KB binaries)
├── rlibc-x2/           # std-compatible replacement (~41 KB binaries)
├── apps/               # Example applications and comparisons
├── tools/              # Development utilities (is-libc-used, func-analysis)
├── xtask/              # Build automation and testing
└── Cargo.toml          # Workspace configuration
```

**Two Approaches:**

| Aspect | rlibc-x1 | rlibc-x2 |
|--------|----------|----------|

The user is asking a great question about why the linker isn't removing unused functions, particularly the `stub!` functions that are clearly never called (since they would exit with 99 if called, but the program exits with 42).

Let me think about this:

1. The `stub!` macro creates functions that exit with code 99
2. These functions are 31 bytes each
3. The func-analysis shows REFS 0 for many functions
4. Despite LTO and optimization, these aren't being removed

There are several possible reasons:

1. **`#[no_mangle]` attribute** - Functions marked with `#[no_mangle]` are typically kept by the linker because they might be called from outside (dynamic linking, C code, etc.). The linker can't prove they won't be called.

Here's the answer:

## Why the linker keeps unused functions

The root cause is **symbol visibility**. Look at this output:

```
Symbol table '.dynsym' contains 67 entries:
...
    47: 0000000000206282    31 FUNC    GLOBAL DEFAULT   11 close
    43: 000000000020637a    31 FUNC    GLOBAL DEFAULT   11 mmap64
```

All your `stub!` functions are:

1. **Marked `#[no_mangle]`** - preserves the exact C symbol name
2. **`extern "C"`** - makes them callable from C code
3. **GLOBAL binding** - visible outside the compilation unit
4. **In the dynamic symbol table** (`.dynsym`) - exported for potential dynamic linking

## The fundamental tension

rlibc-x2's design requires these symbols to be exported:
- Rust's std library references `close`, `mmap64`, `_Unwind_Resume`, etc.
- Your library provides them as replacements for glibc
- The linker must find them, so they must be **globally visible**

But that same visibility prevents dead code elimination:
- LTO and `--gc-sections` treat **exported symbols as roots**
- The linker can't prove they won't be called from outside (e.g., via `dlsym`)
- So it keeps them all

## REFS 0 is correct but irrelevant

`func-analysis` counts internal call/jump references within the binary. REFS 0 means no code *inside* the binary calls them. But the linker doesn't care about that - it sees they're exported and keeps them "just in case."

## Possible solutions

1. **Linker version script** - hide symbols after linking:
   ```
   { global: main; __libc_start_main; local: *; };
   ```

2. **`-fvisibility=hidden`** + explicit exports - but this breaks std's ability to find them

3. **Accept the overhead** - this is the cost of std compatibility (31 bytes × ~30 stubs ≈ 1KB)

4. **Strip `.dynsym`** after linking - but loses debug symbols

The irony: the functions must be visible for std to link against them, but being visible prevents removal. This is an inherent trade-off in the "replace libc" approach.

content.text:
No, the linker **can** do dead code elimination - but only for symbols it considers "internal." Here's the distinction:

## Compiler DCE (Dead Code Elimination)
- Removes unreachable code **within a compilation unit**
- Works on functions with internal linkage (`static` in C, non-`pub` in Rust)
- Happens before the linker sees anything

## Linker DCE (`--gc-sections`)
- Removes **sections** not reachable from "root" symbols
- Requires `-ffunction-sections` (each function in its own section)
- **But**: it starts from "roots" and traces what's reachable

## The problem: what's a "root"?

The linker considers these as roots (can't be eliminated):
- Entry point (`_start`)
- **All exported/GLOBAL symbols**
- Anything marked `--undefined`

Your stub functions are GLOBAL in `.dynsym`:
```
GLOBAL DEFAULT   11 close
GLOBAL DEFAULT   11 mmap64
```

So the linker thinks: "someone outside might call `close()`, I must keep it."

## If they were LOCAL/hidden:

```
LOCAL  DEFAULT   11 close   ← linker could eliminate if unreferenced
```

Then the linker **would** trace from `_start` → `main` → ... and find `close` is never reached, and remove it.

## Summary

| Visibility | Compiler DCE | Linker DCE |
|------------|--------------|------------|
| Internal/static | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| GLOBAL/exported | ❌ No | ❌ No (treated as root) |

The linker is fully capable of DCE - but `#[no_mangle] extern "C"` forces GLOBAL visibility, which tells the linker "this is an entry point, keep it."

Memory at runtime:
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ .dynsym, .dynstr        │ ← Symbol names (loaded but unused)
│ (names like "close")    │
├─────────────────────────┤
│ .text                   │ ← Actual machine code

│   syscall               │
└─────────────────────────┘

The symbol table just maps names → addresses. The **code itself** (31 bytes per stub) is in `.text` and that's what takes space.

content.text:
You're absolutely right, and this is a legitimate criticism of the default toolchain behavior.

## The current model is backwards for executables

For a **shared library** (.so/.dll): exporting symbols makes sense - others will call them.

For an **executable**: nothing can call your internal functions at runtime. The only entry point is `_start`. Yet the linker still treats GLOBAL symbols as "maybe someone will call this."

## What you're proposing

```
Current:  #[no_mangle] → GLOBAL visibility → linker keeps it
Proposed: For executables, treat everything as LOCAL except _start
          Then trace reachability and eliminate REFS 0
```

This would work. The linker already has this capability (`--gc-sections`). The problem is just that GLOBAL symbols are treated as roots.

## Why it's not the default

1. **Historical inertia** - C defaults to external linkage, tools followed
2. **`#[no_mangle]` conflates two things**: "preserve this name" and "export this symbol"
3. **Linker doesn't know intent** - it can't distinguish "I need this name for linking" from "I need this callable at runtime"

## You could actually do this today

```bash
# Linker version script: version.script
{ global: _start; local: *; };

# Link with
-Wl,--version-script=version.script
```

This tells the linker: "only `_start` is a real entry point, localize everything else." Then `--gc-sections` would eliminate your unreachable stubs.

The toolchain supports it - it's just not the default, and Rust doesn't expose visibility control separately from `#[no_mangle]`.

Your point stands: for 99.99% of executables, the current default is wasteful.

content.text:
**There's the problem.** The GOT (Global Offset Table) contains static pointers to:

- `fcntl` (0x204cc1)
- `open64` (0x204d1e)  
- `malloc` (0x204a6e)
- `getauxval` (0x204ce0)
- etc.

## Why DCE fails for these

```
Standard Linker DCE:
  _start → reachable code → KEEP
  
But also:
  .got section → contains pointer to fcntl → KEEP fcntl
  .got section → contains pointer to open64 → KEEP open64
```

The GOT is **data**, not code. The linker sees:
1. `.got` section is referenced (by std's code)
2. `.got` contains addresses of functions
3. Therefore those functions are "reachable" via data pointers

**func-analysis shows REFS 0** because there's no `call fcntl` instruction. But the linker sees the **data pointer** in GOT and keeps it.

## The root cause

Rust's pre-compiled std library was built expecting these libc symbols. It created GOT entries for them. Even with LTO, the boundary between your code and std's pre-compiled code isn't fully optimized.

## Real solutions would require:

1. **Rebuild std with `-Zbuild-std`** - compile std from source with full LTO
2. **Link-time pointer analysis** - prove GOT entries are never dereferenced (very hard)
3. **Different approach entirely** - like `#![no_std]` (rlibc-x1)

Want to try `-Zbuild-std`? That requires nightly but could enable true whole-program optimization.

With `-Zbuild-std`, you compile the standard library from source alongside your code. This means:

content.text:
Yes, in theory. Here's why:

## Without `-Zbuild-std` (current)

```
Your code (compiled with LTO)
        ↓
    Links against
        ↓
Pre-compiled std (already has GOT entries baked in)
        ↓
    Linker sees GOT pointers → keeps functions
```

The LTO boundary stops at std. The GOT entries are already fixed in the pre-compiled std objects.

## With `-Zbuild-std`

```
Your code + std source (compiled together with LTO)
        ↓
    LLVM sees EVERYTHING
        ↓
    Can prove: "this GOT entry is never dereferenced"
        ↓
    Eliminates both the GOT entry AND the function
```

The compiler can do **whole-program optimization** because it sees all the source code, including std internals. It can trace data flow and prove certain paths are dead.

content.thinking:
The user is asking a very good question. If the compiler has all the source code (with -Zbuild-std), why does it still use indirect references (GOT, function pointers) instead of direct calls?

This is a fundamental question about how Rust's std library is designed and how the compiler works.

Let me think about why indirect calls exist even with full source:

1. **Trait objects / dynamic dispatch** - When you have `dyn Trait`, the compiler can't know at compile time which concrete type's method to call. It uses a vtable (table of function pointers). Even with all source code, if the code uses `dyn Trait`, you get indirect calls.

2. **Function pointers as data** - Some designs store function pointers in data structures. For example, panic hooks, thread-local destructors, init arrays, etc. These are patterns in std that use function pointers by design.

3. **Separate compilation model** - Even with LTO, Rust still compiles things in a certain way. The GOT exists because the code was compiled expecting potentially position-independent execution or dynamic linking, even if we're statically linking in the end.

4. **ABI requirements** - Some things like `__libc_start_main` receive `main` as a function pointer argument because that's the C ABI for program startup.

5. **Lazy/conditional initialization** - std uses patterns like `Once` and `OnceLock` that might store function pointers for initialization functions.

The real answer is: Rust's std library was designed with flexibility in mind, using patterns that involve function pointers. Even with all source code available, if the SOURCE CODE uses function pointers, the compiler can't magically turn them into direct calls without whole-program analysis that proves:
1. The pointer always points to one specific function
2. That function can be inlined/devirtualized

LLVM does have some devirtualization passes, but they're limited. They work best when the compiler can prove a specific concrete type, but std uses a lot of generic, flexible patterns that defeat this analysis.


The frustration makes sense—with complete source visibility, one might expect the compiler to eliminate all indirection. But the core issue is that the source code itself is written with these indirect patterns. Determining statically what a function pointer will target is fundamentally difficult and often undecidable. The compiler takes a conservative approach, preserving correctness over aggressive optimization.

content.text:
Excellent question. The issue isn't that the compiler *needs* indirect references - it's that **the source code itself uses them**.

Rust's std library is written with patterns that inherently use function pointers:

## 1. The C ABI startup convention
```rust
// _start calls __libc_start_main(main, argc, argv, ...)
//                        ^^^^
//                        main is passed as a pointer
```
This is baked into how Unix program startup works. `main` is a function pointer argument.

## 2. Trait objects in std
```rust
// std uses dyn Trait for flexibility:
type PanicHandler = dyn Fn(&PanicInfo) + Sync + Send;
```
Even with all source code, `dyn` means "call through vtable" - that's what the keyword *means*.

## 3. Callback patterns
```rust
// std's Once, thread spawning, panic hooks all store function pointers:
static HOOK: AtomicPtr<fn()> = ...;
```

## 4. Init/fini arrays
```rust
#[link_section = ".init_array"]
static INIT: fn() = my_init;  // Function pointer by design
```

## The real problem

The compiler **could** theoretically:
1. See that `HOOK` is only ever set to `foo`
2. Replace all `HOOK()` calls with direct `foo()` calls
3. Eliminate the indirection

But this requires **whole-program pointer analysis** - proving "this pointer only ever holds this one value." LLVM has limited devirtualization, but it's conservative and often fails.

**The source code's design** chose flexibility (function pointers, trait objects) over static dispatch. Even with all source visible, if the code says "store this as a pointer and call through it," the compiler obeys.

The fix would require **rewriting std** to use fewer indirect patterns - which is essentially what `#![no_std]` (rlibc-x1) does.

2. **Dynamic dispatch (explicit)** - Only when you explicitly use `dyn Trait` do you get vtable-based indirect calls.

So the user is right - Rust's default is static dispatch with monomorphization, unlike Java/C++ virtual methods which default to dynamic dispatch.

1. Position-independent code (PIC) - to access global data/functions
2. Dynamic linking - to resolve symbols at runtime

**Your actual Rust main is 3 bytes:**
```asm
mov    $0x2a,%al   ; load 42
ret                ; return
```

But the C `main` wrapper (387 bytes) is doing:
- Thread ID initialization (atomic counter increment)

- Then finally calls your 3-byte function

content.thinking:
Look at all this for a program that just returns 42!- `Once` locks for lazy initialization- `OnceLock` for stdio buffering- `LineWriter` for stdout- `ReentrantLock` for thread safety- Thread ID generation- Exit guardsAll of this is std's runtime infrastructure that gets pulled in because std is designed for multi-threaded programs with I/O.

For a trivial program like ex-x2, none of this is needed. But std doesn't know that at compile time - it conservatively includes this infrastructure.The user's rlibc-x1 approach (no_std) avoids all of this by not using std at all.Maybe we can try to figure out what's actually triggering this... The culprit might be `ExitCode` itself, or just the fact that std's runtime initializes things.

content.text:
All this for `ExitCode::from(42)`:
- `OnceLock<ReentrantLock<RefCell<LineWriter<StdoutRaw>>>>` - stdout buffering
- `std::sync::once::Once` - lazy initialization
- `ThreadId::new::COUNTER` - thread ID generation
- `std::rt::cleanup` - runtime cleanup

std's runtime assumes you **might** do I/O, **might** use threads, **might** need cleanup. So it initializes everything "just in case."
